summary: Laban gives Leah to Jacob after seven years of work promised for Rachel, then gives Rachel after the wedding feast in exchange for another seven years. The chapter traces births through Leah, Rachel, Bilhah, and Zilpah amid unequal affection and rivalry, before describing Jacob's growing flocks and Laban's envy.
whyItMatters: The origins of Jacob's household are told through labor, deception, unequal marriage relationships, and precisely dated births. The narrator also turns the elder-before-younger marriage practice into a law attributed to the heavenly tablets.

context.author: In the book's Sinai frame an angel recounts this material to Moses. That narrative speaker is distinct from the historical author, whom this chapter does not identify.
context.audience: Moses receives the account inside the story for Israel and its descendants. The historical work addresses Jewish concerns about covenant, inherited stories, and observance; a specific first community is uncertain.
context.date: The narrative uses a chronology counted from creation within its Sinai revelation frame. The historical work is usually placed in the second century BCE; an exact composition date is not established.
context.setting: Laban's household and flocks in the land of the east, across successive seven-year periods of Jacob's service.
context.literaryForm: Marriage and birth narrative with chronological notices, a legal interruption, and an account of wages.

before.text: At Bethel Jacob received a promise of protection and vowed a tenth. He now arrives among the relatives to whom Isaac sent him.

here.text: Follow the shift from Laban's marriage bargain to the births of Jacob's children and then to the dispute over his wages.

after.text: Laban's hostility is followed by Jacob's secret departure with his wives, children, and possessions, and by Laban's pursuit.

outline.heading: Leah substituted for Rachel
outline.note: Jacob’s seven years of service end in a marriage he did not expect.

outline.heading: Marriage order becomes law
outline.note: The narrator endorses giving the elder daughter first, and Jacob undertakes another seven years.

outline.heading: Leah’s first sons and Rachel’s distress
outline.note: Births and infertility intensify the unequal relationships in the household.

outline.heading: Births through four women
outline.note: Bilhah, Zilpah, Leah, and Rachel bear the children named and dated here.

outline.heading: Wages, growth, and envy
outline.note: Jacob agrees to remain for livestock wages, prospers, and faces renewed hostility.

keyVerses.text: And Laban said to Jacob: 'It is not so done in our country, to give the younger before the elder.' And it is not right to do this; for thus it is ordained and written in the heavenly tablets, that no one should give his younger daughter before the elder; but the elder, one gives first and after her the younger -and the man who does so, they set down guilt against him in heaven, and none is righteous that does this thing, for this deed is evil before the Lord.
keyVerses.why: A household practice is explicitly elevated into a heavenly rule by the narrator.

keyVerses.text: But the womb of Rachel was closed, for the Lord saw that Leah was hated and Rachel loved.
keyVerses.why: The text relates fertility and infertility to the unequal affection shown to the two sisters.

keyVerses.text: And Laban and his sons envied Jacob, and Laban took back his sheep from him, and he observed him with evil intent.
keyVerses.why: Laban’s envy and seizure of sheep prepare the conflict that prompts departure.

questions.question: Does Jacob wait another seven years before marrying Rachel?
questions.answer: No. Laban gives Rachel after the seven days of Leah's feast, and Jacob then serves the additional seven years. The chapter distinguishes the wedding week from the longer period of labor.

questions.question: Does the heavenly rule excuse everything Laban does?
questions.answer: The narrator supports the rule that the elder daughter should be married first, while Jacob explicitly calls Laban's substitution wrong. The chapter does not resolve the ethical difference between following a marriage order and deceiving the intended husband.

questions.question: What does “week” mean in the opening chronology?
questions.answer: The first verse says Jacob serves one week, and the next identifies this as seven years. Later the text also speaks of seven days of a wedding feast, so the unit must be read from its immediate context.

questions.question: Does Rachel’s infertility mean infertile people are being punished?
questions.answer: The narrator specifically connects Rachel's closed womb and Leah's fertility with Jacob's unequal love. That explanation belongs to this family story; it cannot establish a general cause of infertility or a judgment on people experiencing it.

questions.question: What place do Bilhah and Zilpah have in the family?
questions.answer: They are described as handmaids supplied by Laban and then given to Jacob as wives to bear children. Their voices and consent are not recorded, an important limit when reading a story shaped by household status and reproductive expectations.

questions.question: Why are so many dates attached to the births?
questions.answer: The notices locate the children within the work's system of jubilees, weeks, years, months, and days. Some notices move back to an earlier year, so their order in the paragraph should not automatically be treated as a simple chronological list.

questions.question: How does Jacob become wealthy, and why does trouble follow?
questions.answer: Laban agrees that certain marked lambs and kids will be Jacob's wages, and those animals multiply. Jacob gains many possessions, but Laban and his sons envy him and Laban takes sheep back, creating the pressure for the next departure.

glossary.def: The authoritative heavenly record to which the narrator attributes the rule about marrying the elder daughter first.
A female household servant; Bilhah and Zilpah are also made wives and bear children in this narrative.
The agreed return for Jacob’s labor, first connected with marriage and later with marked livestock.
